sentence: Because the road ahead is narrower than the cell.
claim: A red cell is about 7.5 µm across, yet it passes microvessels only about 3 µm wide, so the vessels ahead of it can be narrower than the cell.
source_title: Red blood cells are highly deformable (University of Rochester, Biomedical Engineering)
note: Excerpt: highly deformable, 'which enables them to traverse microvessels whose diameter is only about 3µm'.

sentence: Meet a red blood cell: a dimpled disc, about seven and a half micrometers.
claim: Red blood cells are dimpled (biconcave) discs, 7–8 µm across.
note: Excerpt gives 7–8 µm and 'they lack a nucleus, organelles, and cannot divide'. Other texts give 7.5–8 µm. The scale pill on the hero reads 7.5 µm at the same moment. 26 Oct audit (independent fact check): 'about seven' became 'about seven and a half' so the voice and the 7.5 µm pill agree.

sentence: It even pushed out its own nucleus.
claim: A maturing mammalian red blood cell expels its nucleus (enucleation), so mature red cells have none. In the Whitehead study (mouse erythroblasts), a contracting ring of actin pinches the nucleus off and macrophages clear it.
source_title: Whitehead Institute, How red blood cells nuke their nuclei
note: Rewritten 24 Oct with the script (v2). The biconcave shape moved into c2. 26 Oct audit: the actin ring is reported in mouse, not human, erythroblasts (a 2024 review), so the claim no longer calls it general; the voiced line, 'pushed out its own nucleus', is unchanged.

sentence: You have about twenty-five trillion of them: most of your own cells.
claim: A reference adult has about 30 trillion human cells, about 84% of them red blood cells (about 25 trillion). The body also holds about 38 trillion bacteria, hence 'your own cells'.
source_title: BioNumbers 113005: distribution of cell number and mass by cell type (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLOS Biology)
note: Cross-check fix applied: 'most of the cells in your body' was false once bacteria count. The 84% share is from BioNumbers' excerpt of the paper's figure and Medical News Today; 0.84 × 30 trillion = 25.2 trillion (computed).

sentence: Follow it as the vessel branches, and branches again, into a capillary.
claim: Arteries branch into smaller vessels, the arterioles, which feed capillary beds.
source_title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, chapter 20 review (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt: 'Arteries transport blood away from the heart and branch into smaller vessels, forming arterioles. Arterioles distribute blood to capillary beds, the sites of exchange with the body tissues.'

sentence: There's no room to overtake, so cells go through in single file.
claim: The narrowest microvessels (about 3 µm) are smaller than a red cell, and in capillaries red cells travel in single file.
source_title: Red blood cells are highly deformable (University of Rochester, Biomedical Engineering)
note: Excerpt: 'in capillaries, red blood cells travel in single file separated by plasma gaps'.

claim: Squeezing through narrow capillaries, a red cell deforms at constant volume and nearly constant surface area: its membrane strongly resists stretching.
source_title: Halpern & Secomb 1989, The squeezing of red blood cells through capillaries with near-minimal diameters, J. Fluid Mech. 203:381
note: The membrane strongly resists stretching: a squeezed red cell keeps nearly constant surface area, so it folds rather than stretches (the wrong guess the line sets up). 26 Oct audit (independent fact check): the wrong guess now says 'its surface stretches to fit': a red cell does lengthen easily (optical-tweezer studies stretch it); what it can't do is grow its membrane area (lysis at about 2–4% area expansion). The guess and its correction are now the same idea, and match this claim.

sentence: The dimples give it spare surface for its volume, so it folds into a parachute instead.
claim: A red cell's surface-area-to-volume ratio, more than its stiffness, decides how narrow a passage it can get through.
source_title: Namvar et al., Surface area-to-volume ratio, not cellular viscoelasticity, is the major determinant of red blood cell traversal through small channels, Cellular Microbiology 23(1):e13270 (University of Melbourne record)
note: 'Spare surface for its volume' is the standard reading of that ratio (a sphere of the same volume has less surface). Excerpt (abstract): 'Dramatic stiffening of RBCs had no measurable effect on their ability to traverse small channels', while 'a moderate decrease in the SA:V ratio had a marked effect'. 26 Oct audit (independent fact check): cited as the peer-reviewed paper (DOI 10.1111/cmi.13270) instead of its bioRxiv preprint (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.07.11.191494.full.pdf, 'not cellular rigidity').

sentence: The dimples give it spare surface for its volume, so it folds into a parachute instead.
claim: In capillary flow, a red cell changes from a disc to a parachute shape as the flow speeds up.
source_title: Noguchi & Gompper 2005, Shape transitions of fluid vesicles and red blood cells in capillary flows, PNAS 102:14159
note: Excerpt (PMC1242298 abstract): 'a model RBC is found to transit from a nonaxisymmetric discocyte to an axisymmetric parachute shape'. A simulation that the authors report agrees with experiments.

sentence: The tightest vessels are about three micrometers: less than half its width.
claim: Red cells traverse microvessels only about 3 µm across, about 40% of a 7.5 µm cell.
source_title: Red blood cells are highly deformable (University of Rochester, Biomedical Engineering)
note: Cross-check fix: replaces the unsupported 'only about half its width' [S3, PMC8215585]. 3 / 7.5 = 0.40 (computed). 26 Oct audit (independent fact check): 'The tightest' became 'The tightest vessels' (heard after a silent hold, the noun was missing).

sentence: And it keeps squeezing through, all its life: about a hundred and twenty days.
claim: A red blood cell lives about 120 days on average.
source_title: Erythrocyte Aging, MeSH (US National Library of Medicine)
note: Excerpt: 'This limits the average life span of an erythrocyte to 120 days.'

sentence: Sickle cells lose the disc shape, stiffen, and can jam where oxygen is handed out.
claim: Capillary beds are extremely narrow, which slows red cells and gives gas exchange time to happen.
source_title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, 18.3 Erythrocytes (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt: 'Capillary beds are extremely narrow, slowing the passage of the erythrocytes and providing an extended opportunity for gas exchange to occur.' 26 Oct audit (independent fact check): the line was 'Stiff sickle cells can jam the smallest vessels…'; it now names the lost disc shape (the link to the dimple) and drops 'the smallest vessels'.

sentence: Meanwhile, as you watched, your bone marrow made over a hundred million new red cells.
claim: The body makes about two million red blood cells every second, in the bone marrow.
source_title: Blood cells (MedlinePlus, US National Library of Medicine)
note: Excerpt: 'The body makes about two million red blood cells every second!' The tally is 2,000,000 × t from frame 0; the line starts at about 59 s (about 118 million), and 'over a hundred million' holds for any start after 50 s (computed). Consistent with 25 trillion cells / 120 days = 2.4 million a second (computed).

sentence: Room for about a billion passengers.
claim: A red blood cell holds about 270 million hemoglobin molecules.
source_title: Hemoglobin and heme products (Merck technical article)
note: Excerpt: '~270 million hemoglobin molecules' per cell; Wikipedia's red blood cell article gives the same. The cross-check found 250–300 million across sources, so the product is 1.0–1.2 billion: 'about a billion' holds. 270 million × 4 = 1.08 billion (computed).

sentence: Room for about a billion passengers.
claim: Each hemoglobin has four heme groups, each binding one oxygen molecule: four O₂ per hemoglobin.
source_title: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids
note: Excerpt: hemoglobin is 'made of four subunits'; 'each heme group that contains iron binds one oxygen molecule'.

sentence: Sickle cells lose the disc shape, stiffen, and can jam where oxygen is handed out.
claim: In sickle cell disease, red cells take a sickle or crescent shape instead of a disc shape; they are stiff and sticky, don't bend or move easily, and can clog capillaries and block blood flow.
note: Excerpt (NHLBI): sickle cell disease 'causes the red blood cells to have a sickle or crescent shape instead of a disc shape'; healthy cells are disc-shaped and flexible, sickled cells 'do not bend or move easily and can block blood flow'. MIT News, 1 March 2012 (https://news.mit.edu/2012/sickle-cell-blood-flow-0301), excerpt: 'crescent-shaped red blood cells that clog capillaries instead of flowing smoothly, like ordinary, disc-shaped red blood cells do.' NHLBI fact sheet (July 2022, https://internet-prod.nhlbi.nih.gov/sites/default/files/publications/SickleCellDisease_FactSheet_July2022.pdf), earlier excerpt: 'rigid strands … clogging the capillaries' (the audit could not re-find that phrase; a person checks it). 'Can' keeps it to what the sources say; the cause is hemoglobin S, not the dimple. 'Where oxygen is handed out' points at the capillaries, which NHLBI and MIT both name; a 2012 Drexel study places much obstruction just downstream of them. 26 Oct audit (independent fact check): rewritten from 'Stiff sickle cells can jam the smallest vessels' so the takeaway's button ('That dimple isn't decoration') follows: sickle cells lose the disc.

claim: In a microfluidic study, the surface-area-to-volume ratio that the biconcave disc provides was the major determinant of how narrow a channel a red cell could pass: a moderate loss of it markedly narrowed what cells could get through, while dramatic stiffening alone had no measurable effect in those channels.
source_title: Namvar et al., Surface area-to-volume ratio, not cellular viscoelasticity, is the major determinant of red blood cell traversal through small channels, Cellular Microbiology 23(1):e13270 (University of Melbourne record)
note: Excerpt (abstract): 'a moderate decrease in the SA:V ratio had a marked effect on the equivalent cylinder diameter traversable by RBCs of similar cellular viscoelasticity'; 'the SA:V ratio should be given more prominence in studies of RBC pathologies'. 26 Oct audit (independent fact check): the line was tagged {-}, but it asserts that the shape has a function, so it now carries this claim.
